editor_spans.body: The Motherwell speech complicates our earlier reading that Andy Burnham's offer to Holyrood is aimed only at Edinburgh's powers. Its one concrete item is London's to give: 'DWP devolution', a localised employment-support model 'shaped by Holyrood'. He also floats devolving UK innovation, enterprise and employability funding. These are reserved levers, not Scottish ones.

The pressure still points in one direction, though. Westminster offers to hand down some of its own money and programmes. Holyrood is asked to hand down far more: skills, transport, housing and infrastructure decisions to Scotland's regions. Its existing local government reform is waved aside with 'we've got to move faster'.

Burnham diagnoses Scotland as 'one of the most centralised nations in Europe' but never says how it got there. Much of that centralisation was built at Holyrood over two decades. Successive Scottish governments held down council tax for years, merged local police and fire services into national bodies, and ran employability schemes from the centre. Any regional settlement would have to reverse those choices. That is a harder ask of John Swinney than matching £10 million for two defence colleges.

The test comes quickly. In 'a couple of weeks' the National Economic Council meets the devolved First Ministers for the first time under this Prime Minister. If the DWP offer arrives with conditions about how Holyrood must pass power down to the regions, it will be read in Edinburgh as leverage, not partnership. The speech's language of 'open hands' will not settle that.

One line is more revealing than it sounds. Burnham warns that Scottish towns risk being 'underpowered' while northern English city regions 'power up'. He is setting up a competition between the English mayoral model and Holyrood's centralism. That comparison will be made every time an English mayor gets a power a Scottish council does not, and that may matter more than this particular offer.
